questions.question: You want to show two vertices are connected, and a proof would be easier with a path than a walk. Is it safe to assume the connection is a path?
options: No, a walk may exist when no path does
Yes, a shortest walk between them never repeats a vertex, so it is a path
Only if the graph is a tree
Only if the walk has length at most 3
questions.explanation: If a shortest walk repeated a vertex, you could cut out the loop and get a shorter walk. So a shortest walk is always a path, in any graph.

questions.question: A connected graph has vertex degrees 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 2. What is the best you can do?
options: An Euler tour that returns to the start
An Euler walk that starts at one degree-3 vertex and ends at the other
An Euler walk that can start anywhere
questions.explanation: There are exactly two odd-degree vertices, so an open Euler walk exists. It is forced to begin at one odd vertex and finish at the other.

questions.question: How does the lecture prove the open Euler walk theorem without redoing the long tour proof?
options: By strong induction on the number of edges
By deleting one of the odd vertices
By adding a new vertex joined to both odd vertices, taking an Euler tour, then removing the new vertex
questions.explanation: This is a reduction. The extra vertex makes every degree even, the tour theorem applies, and deleting the extra vertex turns the tour into the desired walk.

questions.question: A connected graph has 10 vertices and 10 edges. What can you conclude?
options: It contains at least one cycle
It has at least two leaves
questions.explanation: A tree on 10 vertices has exactly 9 edges. Being connected with 10 edges means the graph is not a tree, so it must have a cycle. Nothing forces leaves or even degrees.
